meltdown.que: An involuntary response to sensory, emotional, or cognitive overload that exceeds the nervous system's limit. It's not a tantrum or a voluntary act: the brain is literally overflowing.
signos: Hitting, biting, or mild self-injury (urgent self-stimulation)
Rigidity or shaking in the body
ayuda: Don't speak or touch unless the person asks
Wait without judgment until the nervous system settles
Afterward, don't ask for an immediate explanation
meltdown.tts: If you're in a meltdown right now, what's happening isn't something you're doing on purpose. It's your nervous system hitting its limit after too much load. There may be crying, screaming, a need to move or to flee. All of that is an involuntary response, not a failure on your part. What helps most right now is reducing what's coming in: turn off lights, lower the sound, step away from people if you can. You don't need to explain anything right now. Regulate first, talk later.

shutdown.que: A closing-down response to overload: the nervous system "shuts off" to protect itself. Unlike a meltdown, a shutdown turns inward — silence, stillness, disconnection.
ayuda: Calm presence without demanding a response
Don't read the silence as indifference
Offer blankets, headphones, or comfort objects
Once it passes, gently ask what they need
shutdown.tts: In a shutdown your nervous system closes down to protect itself from overload. It's not that you don't want to respond, it's that you can't. Staying silent, still, or disconnected isn't indifference, it's survival. Don't push yourself to snap out of it. What helps is a calm environment, no questions or demands, with some comfort nearby if you're open to it: a blanket, headphones, darkness. Your nervous system will come back at its own pace.

burnout.que: A state of deep exhaustion caused by the sustained effort of masking, adapting to a neurotypical world, and handling a sensory and social load beyond available resources. It can last weeks or months.
signos: Losing skills that used to be automatic
Exhaustion that doesn't improve with usual rest
ayuda: Seek professional support experienced with autism
Allow yourself to function at a slower pace without guilt
burnout.tts: Autistic burnout is the result of giving too much for too long, trying to fit into a world that isn't built for you. It's not laziness or depression, even though it can look like it. You might notice things you used to do without thinking now take a huge effort. That's normal in burnout. The most important thing right now is to reduce what you can: commitments, demands, the effort of masking. Give yourself permission to function more slowly. Seek support if you can, ideally from someone who understands autism. Recovery takes time, and that's okay.

Frío.desc: Cold water on wrists and face, ice in your hands or on your forehead. Triggers the dive reflex and slows the nervous system.
Frío.tts: If you're feeling overwhelmed, cold can help you regulate very quickly. Put cold water on your wrists and face, or hold an ice cube in your hand. You'll notice the effect within seconds: cold triggers the dive reflex and tells the nervous system to slow down.

Respiración.desc: Exhale twice as long as you inhale. 4 sec. in, 8 out. Activates the vagus nerve and regulates heart rate.
Respiración.tts: Exhale twice as long as you inhale. Four seconds breathing in, eight breathing out. That long exhale activates the vagus nerve and regulates your heart rate. If four and eight feels like too much, start with two and four. What matters is that the out-breath is slow.

Movimiento.desc: Jumping, squeezing a ball, clenching your fists, stretching. Proprioceptive movement calms the nervous system.
Movimiento.tts: When your body feels overloaded, moving helps release tension. Jump, squeeze a ball, clench your fists, or stretch. This kind of movement signals to the nervous system that everything is under control and helps it calm down.

Sonido.desc: Earplugs, noise-canceling headphones, or background sound (rain, white noise). Reduces auditory sensory load.
Sonido.tts: If the environment is too loud, cover your ears. Use earplugs or noise-canceling headphones. You can also play background sound like rain or white noise. Reducing auditory load frees up resources your nervous system can use to regulate.

Oscuridad.desc: Covering your eyes, sunglasses, or a dark room. Removes visual overload and gives a sense of shelter.
Oscuridad.tts: Darkness can be a shelter when overload is visual. Cover your eyes, put on sunglasses, or find a dark room. Removing visual stimulation gives your brain the break it needs.

Presión.desc: A weighted blanket, a snug jacket, or simply hugging your knees. Deep pressure regulates the nervous system.
Presión.tts: Deep pressure is very calming for the nervous system. Use a weighted blanket, put on a snug jacket, or simply hug your own knees. You'll notice arousal drop and your body start to relax.

Sabor intenso.desc: A sour candy, gum, ice. Strong oral stimulation pulls the nervous system's attention to one single thing.
Sabor intenso.tts: A very strong flavor can anchor the nervous system's attention to one single thing and break the overload loop. Eat a sour candy, chew gum, or hold ice in your mouth. The stronger the flavor, the more effective the anchor.

Grounding 5-4-3.desc: Name 5 things you see, 4 you touch, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste. Anchors you in the present.
Grounding 5-4-3.tts: If you're stuck in your head and need to come back to the present, name five things you can see right now, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, and one you can taste. You don't have to say it out loud, just noticing them is enough. Every sense you engage lowers nervous-system arousal.

Salida.desc: Changing environment — stepping into a hallway, bathroom, or outside. Sometimes the only regulator is breaking the stimulus.
Salida.tts: Sometimes the only regulator available is changing your environment. If you can, leave the space you're in: a hallway, the bathroom, outside. Stepping away from the stimulus breaks the overload cycle and gives your nervous system a cleaner starting point.

pequeno.label: Small bag
pequeno.tts: Small bag for emergencies. What to pack: headphones or earplugs to block noise, sunglasses for bright light, sour candy for oral regulation, a textured object for your hands, your crisis card with your information and needs, and a charged phone.

grande.label: Large bag
grande.tts: Large bag for long outings. Pack active noise-canceling headphones, sunglasses, sensory snacks like candy or gum, a fidget toy for your hands, your crisis card, your phone with a portable charger, cold water for cold-based regulation, an eye mask in case you need emergency darkness, your medication if you take it regularly, and something to distract you like a book or a device.

enorme.label: Large backpack
enorme.tts: Large backpack for hard days or trips. Bring the best noise-canceling headphones you have, polarized sunglasses, a sensory assortment with different flavors and textures, several fidgets of different types and weights, your crisis or communication support cards, your phone with a high-capacity power bank, cold water and snacks for hydration and regulation, a small blanket for weight or tactile comfort, an eye mask for emergency darkness, your medication with an extra dose if your doctor approves, some entertainment like a console, book, or tablet, your favorite perfume or scent for olfactory stimulation, spare earplugs in case your headphones fail, and comfortable spare clothes in case your current fabric becomes intolerable.

items.label: Medication
items.nota: With extra dose if your doctor approves

items.label: Extra comfortable clothes
items.nota: In case the fabric becomes intolerable
